title: Center without Walls for Imaging Proteinopathies with PET
text:
This competing renewal requests continued support for the U19 “Center without Walls” entitled “Center
Without Walls for Imaging Proteinopathies with PET”. This Center consists of the scientific integration of
individuals with an international reputation in the fields of neurobiology, neurology, medicinal chemistry,
PET radiochemistry and CNS PET imaging studies towards the common goal of developing PET
radiotracers for imaging aggregated alpha synuclein and 4R tau, and investigating their role in
neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson’s disease (PD), Multiple System Atrophy (MSA) and
Frontotemporal Dementia. The scientific resources created by the funding of this U19 Center has led to
the first application of the use of ultrahigh throughput screening of large in silico compound libraries in
PET radiotracer development. Two radiotracers for imaging alpha synuclein in MSA and PD have been
translated to date to the Clinical Core; a third radiotracer for 4R tau is anticipated in year 5 of the current
application. The radiotracers developed by this U19 Center are expected to have an important impact on
the scientific mission of the National Institute on Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) in the study
of the synucleinopathies and 4R tauopathies.

title: Function of HIV-1 Env cytoplasmic tail domain
text:
The long-term objective of the proposed research is to increase our knowledge about the structure, function
and inhibition of the HIV-1 Env, the major surface protein on the virion responsible for viral attachment and
entry. This application proposes to explore the molecular mechanisms that guide Env in infected cells to sites
of new virus formation and/or sites that support cell-to-cell virus transfer. The research will ultimately facilitate
therapeutic development for the treatment and prevention of AIDS.

title: Core A Mouse Genetics and Genomics Core
text: Core A: Mouse Genetics and Genomics (Core Leader: Ferris) Abstract Mouse models of human diseases, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), have proven invaluable for understanding the underlying genetic, molecular and physiological or immunological basis of these disease processes. Recent work has shown that mouse models that incorporate population-wide genetic diversity can model unique aspects of the response to Mtb infection, as well as immunization against Mtb, with several of these strains recapitulating unique aspects of human disease. The mouse genetics core serves this larger program by identifying/confirming the genetic features driving these unique aspects of host responses to Mtb via experimental crosses and infection or immunization studies between mouse strains segregating candidate genome regions, concurrent with genomic and transcriptomic refinement of the candidate variants and pathways. Lastly, the core will incorporate the results of these analyses to generate improved models of Mtb disease via the generation of new congenic or mutant mouse strains for the research projects to dissect the impact of these models and genetically variable pathways on Mtb disease.

title: Adversarially Based Virtual CT Workflow for Evaluation of AI in Medical Imaging
text:
The overall goal of this academic-FDA partnership R01 project is to generate diverse training and challenging
testing datasets of low-dose CT (LDCT) scans, prototype a virtual CT workflow, and establish an evaluation
methodology for AI-based imaging products to support FDA marketing authorization. Upon completion, our
Adversarially Based CT (ABC) workflow/platform will be made publicly available, and readily extendable to
other imaging modalities and other diseases. This ABC system will be shared through the FDA’s Catalog of
Regulatory Science Tools, and uniquely well positioned to greatly facilitate the development, assessment, and
translation of emerging AI-based imaging products.

title: Using the gut microbiome to treat disuse atrophy in aging.
text:
Skeletal muscle atrophy caused by inactivity/disuse affects young and old individuals alike; however, the full
recovery of muscle mass and function is compromised in the elderly. The purpose of this proposal is to
determine if substances made by the gut microbiome are able to prevent muscle atrophy during limb
immobilization and enhance the recovery of muscle size and strength after disuse.

title: Syphilis Immunology and Biology to Improve Clinical Management and Vaccine Design
text:
A planned longitudinal cohort study will enroll individuals to study the immunological response to
syphilis infection and transcriptome of Treponema (T.) pallidum, the bacterium that causes
syphilis, using state-of-the-art omics approaches. Our proposed study is a continuation of our
current work and will inform global syphilis research and advance knowledge of syphilis
pathogenesis toward improving diagnostics and vaccine development.

title: Cell and Tissue Imaging Shared Resources (CTISR)
text: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT – CELL AND TISSUE IMAGING SHARED RESOURCE The mission of the Cell and Tissue Imaging Shared Resource (CTISR) is to drive and accelerate the use of advanced imaging technologies by St. Jude Comprehensive Cancer Center (SJCCC) members. The CTISR is composed of a Light Microscopy section, led by Aaron Taylor, PhD, and an Electron Microscopy section, led by Camenzind Robinson, PhD. Together, Taylor and Robinson have more than 35 years of experience as imaging scientists. The CTISR is staffed by 10 scientists, four of whom hold PhDs. In addition to offering state-of-the-art commercial instrumentation, the CTISR provides expert, end-to-end support for a wide range of imaging workflows, including whole-organ imaging with tissue clearing, multicolor localization microscopy with data analysis, expansion microscopy, pre- and post-embedding correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM), array tomography, negative staining, immunogold labeling, and high-pressure freezing with freeze substitution. The CTISR works collaboratively with SJCCC members, beginning with a consultation on project needs, followed by hands-on training, and ending with support throughout execution of each imaging experiment, often including assistance with custom data analysis. CTISR staff also validate new methods prior to dissemination to ensure that end users can succeed on their first try. During FY2024, the CTISR provided services to 100 investigators at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. Of these 58 (58%) were SJCCC members from four of the five research Programs, contributing to 66% of the chargebacks. Educational workshops were also held to increase awareness of the CTISR’s capabilities, especially amongst trainees. During the project period, the CTISR contributed to 117 publications authored by SJCCC members, of which 35 (30%) were interprogrammatic and 33 (28%) were intraprogrammatic. CTISR staff were coauthors on 24 (15%) of the publications, signifying the value of their expertise to the research presented. Of the publications supported by the CTISR, 75 (64%) were in high-impact journals (impact factor >10), such as Cell, Nature, and Nature Genetics. During the next project period, the CTISR plans to evolve its correlative light and electron microscopy services while expanding into the new Inspiration4 Advanced Research Center, where light microscopes are located with a high-pressure freezer to facilitate cryogenic CLEM workflows. Additional staff also will be hired to strengthen the continuity of operations and to enable senior CTISR staff to spend more time on educational outreach and methods development and validation.

title: Structural mechanisms of respiratory syncytial virus and human metapneumovirus assembly
text:
Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) and Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) cause severe lung infections, which
may lead to other illnesses or death, and we urgently need better ways to fight them. The proposed structural
studies will utilize advanced imaging technologies to reveal, in unprecedented detail, the native structures of
these viruses and their component parts, as well as how they assemble within infected cells and spread from
one cell to another. By understanding these fundamental processes, we aim to discover new targets for
developing life-saving antiviral drugs and therapeutics.

title: INTERPERSONAL STRESS EXPERIENCES AND HAZARDOUS DRINKING AMONG HISPANIC ADULTS
text:
Hazardous drinking and anxiety among Hispanic persons in the United States represent important public
health concerns. The proposed research aims to study whether interpersonal stress experiences are
associated with alcohol use motivation, hazardous drinking, and anxiety experiences among Hispanic
individuals who engage in hazardous drinking and explore mediational processes and moderators in these
relations. Findings may improve understanding of modifiable psychosocial factors associated with hazardous
drinking and anxiety and inform future intervention development.

title: Hybrid Tissue Engineering Constructs for Enhancing Distraction Osteogenesis
text:
Distraction osteogenesis (DO) is a widely used surgical procedure as treatment for a variety of bone issues:
large bone defects, non-union, persistent bone infection, or congenital or post-trauma limb length discrepancies.
Although the DO procedure has been proven to be an effective method to stimulate new bone formation, there
are complications, such as the long duration due to prolonged consolidation. We envision that our proposed
tissue engineering approach will address these challenges and significantly improve treatment outcomes for
large bone defects, limb deformity, and limb salvage.

title: Improving bacterial cancer therapeutics
text:
Bacteria programmed to make anti-cancer drugs will grow inside tumors but not normal organs,
which means they can be used to specifically deliver drugs to tumors and metastases and
reduce side effects. However, bacteria don’t colonize human tumors very well, and we don’t
really understand why. We will use many strains of bacteria with mutations in different genes to
see which genes affect colonization of tumors, which will let us make anti-cancer bacteria that
are even more specific to tumors.

title: High-throughput functional analyses of the genetic drivers of Inflammatory Bowel Disease
text:
Research into the genetic factors influencing the functioning of the human intestine contributes to fundamental
knowledge about the intricate physiology of living systems. By unraveling the drivers of development of
Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), this research enhances understanding of how intestinal physiology and
function are regulated to maintain homeostasis. In the long term, it paves the way for precise therapies that
could significantly improve the well-being, longevity, and quality of life for individuals with IBD, addressing a
major health concern.

title: Mapping Molecular Exposomics: From Blood Biomarkers to Tissue Architecture
text:
Environmental exposures (collectively as the “exposome”) drive major chronic disease risks, yet current
methods only capture a tiny portion of the human chemical exposures and destroy critical spatial information
about how chemicals accumulate in tissues to cause disease. This project develops an integrated molecular
exposomics platform that comprehensively profiles thousands of chemicals in blood, maps their precise
distributions within human tissues at cellular resolution, and establishes quantitative relationships linking
systemic exposures to tissue-specific pathology. By revealing the hidden geography of environmental exposure
from circulation through tissue architecture to molecular perturbations, this transformative platform will enable
precision environmental health interventions tailored to individual exposure profiles, fundamentally shifting
medicine from reactive treatment to predictive prevention based on a comprehensive molecular understanding
of exposure-disease relationships.

title: Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Shared Resource
text: BIOSTATISTICS AND BIOINFORMATICS SHARED RESOURCE: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT The Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Shared Resource (BBSR) supports the mission of the Wilmot Cancer Institute (Wilmot) by providing biostatistics and bioinformatics services and collaboration through consulting, data analysis, targeted novel methodological development, education, training, and mentoring. The BBSR is co-led by Derick Peterson, PhD (ZY), co-director for biostatistics, and Matthew McCall, PhD (GEM), co-director for bioinformatics. Peterson and McCall are assisted by seven additional biostatisticians and bioinformaticians (three PhD, three MS, and one BS). BBSR faculty and staff collaborate with all three Wilmot research programs, with over 49% of Wilmot members making use of BBSR services since 2019. Additionally, since 2019, the BBSR has supported 148 manuscript submissions and 195 grant proposals, while assisting in the design of 87 investigator-initiated studies with Wilmot investigators. Wilmot’s research environment is strengthened via BBSR support for study design and planning, protocol development and review, grant preparation, statistical modeling and inference, and interpretation and dissemination of study results via manuscripts, abstracts, and scientific presentations. The BBSR develops novel statistical and bioinformatic methods and tools to address unique analysis problems that can emerge from cutting-edge cancer research. This capability positions the BBSR as a leader within the Wilmot research community. Education, training, and mentoring in study design and statistical and bioinformatic approaches elevates collaboration and fosters integration and communication with and between all research programs and shared resources. By providing these services in a cost-effective, highly responsive, and easily accessible fashion, the BBSR serves an integral role in supporting cancer research at Wilmot. Early, in-depth, and sustained involvement in the design and conduct of externally funded studies is key to successful collaboration. BBSR personnel regularly attend monthly Wilmot program meetings and weekly scientific lab meetings with Wilmot investigators to foster and maintain close collaborative relationships with an open flow of communication. This includes defining outcome variables and important covariates, developing appropriate measures and methods to obtain the relevant data necessary to properly answer study questions, focusing and refining specific aims, identifying appropriate biostatistics and bioinformatics methods for data analysis and summarization, leveraging advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence, performing power and sample size calculations, and conveying the results of these analyses via reports, tables, and figures. The BBSR also plays a critical role in clinical research via participation in the Wilmot Protocol Review and Monitoring Committee, the Data and Safety Monitoring Committee, and the Clinical Research Leadership Committee. Moving forward, the BBSR will enhance services and methodological support in imaging analysis and data integration, strengthen bioinformatic capabilities, and expand investigator education.

title: Hawaii IDeA Center for Pediatric and Adolescent Clinical Trials3 (HIPACT3)
text: Facilitating clinical trials in Hawaii with the participation of Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander population, as well as children living in rural communities, creates an opportunity to study disease process and the impact of medical intervention in a high risk population. Insights from these clinical trials and the dissemination of the knowledge in Hawaii will positively affect clinical practice, enhance the quality of healthcare delivery, better patient outcomes, and improve the overall health and well-being of all children living in Hawaii.

title: Dissecting regulation and function of unc-6/Netrin via the generation of cis-regulatory alleles
text:
UNC-6/Netrin plays vital roles in the directing of neuronal axons to their target cells, as well as in the
formation of synapses, the connections between neurons that permit communication between them. It
is unknown, though, whether the neurons that express unc-6/Netrin for the purpose of axon
pathfinding are the same as those that express unc-6/Netrin to facilitate synapse formation. I propose
to use the roundworm C. elegans to determine whether these two functions are separable and to
characterize neuron-specific control of unc-6/Netrin expression, which may help me to elucidate the
relative contribution of the lack of each of these functions in unc-6/Netrin-associated
neurodevelopmental diseases.

title: Biomarker guided combinations for treating high-risk bladder cancer
text:
This study addresses the unsolved problem of chemotherapy resistance in advanced cancers through evidence-
based treatment combinations that target Chase, an enzyme first of its kind. Chase renders the common
chemotherapy drug Gemcitabine ineffective. Development of the combinations concurrently with the evaluation
of Chase and related molecules as predictors of treatment response could enable the clinical translation of these
combinations for the treatment of high-risk, advanced bladder cancers.

title: East Africa International Epidemiology Database to evaluate AIDS (IeDEA) Regional Consortium
text:
Through our efforts, we will enhance our understanding of the HIV care cascades and the outcomes of care
in East Africa, provide insights on the optimal structure and impact of care and treatment programs, expand
the set of tools available to inform implementation and operations research in resource-constrained settings
and inform policy among stakeholders and decision makers at every level in the region as well as the
broader HIV/AIDS scientific community.

title: Molecular Glues for 14-3-3 and ChREBPalpha: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential for protecting pancreatic beta-cells
text:
Diabetes affects over 500 million people worldwide and leads to progressive loss of insulin-producing β-cells,
which current therapies cannot prevent. This project targets a stress-induced molecular pathway by stabilizing
the interaction between ChREBPα and 14-3-3 proteins, which prevents ChREBPα from entering the nucleus and
activating expression of the harmful ChREBPβ isoform. By blocking this feedforward loop that drives β-cell
failure, the proposed work aims to preserve β-cell identity and function in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

title: Targeting Intrinsic and Extrinsic Barriers to RGC and Optic Nerve Regeneration
text:
This research addresses fundamental barriers to neural repair in the visual system, with the goal of advancing
novel strategies for treating traumatic optic nerve injury and other acute optic neuropathies. By uncovering the
key molecular and cellular mechanisms that limit retinal ganglion cell regeneration, this project aims to inform
new approaches for restoring vision after injury. The proposed studies have the potential to improve patient
outcomes and reduce the long-term impact of central nervous system trauma.
